newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan delegate, China leader could meet at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan delegate, China leader could meet at APEC.

text.p: Taiwan said on Monday its top China negotiator would attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, opening the door to a rare encounter with China's leaders after 17 months of sometimes hostile tensions.

Koo Chen-fu, chairman of Taiwan's state-financed Straits Exchange Foundation and a senior member of the ruling Nationalist Party, would represent President Lee Teng-hui at the APEC summit in the Philippines, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
The host country, under public pressure from China, has rejected Taiwan's request that Lee or Vice-President Lien Chan be allowed to attend.

China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and strives to isolate Lee and his exiled Chinese Nationalist government. Taiwan sits in APEC as a customs territory, not a sovereign state.

Koo's presence at the November 25-26 Subic Bay summit would afford a chance to meet Chinese President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin and other senior Beijing officials -- a rare opportunity for a direct exchange of views.

Koo, billionaire head of one of Taiwan's biggest business conglomerates, Koo's Group, represented Lee at the November 1995 APEC summit in Osaka, Japan, but exchanged nothing more than a tense handshake with Jiang.

At that time, tensions across the Taiwan strait were rapidly worsening as Beijing mounted round after round of missile tests and war games in waters near Taiwan in what it called a warning to the island not to stray from the path towards reunification.
Taipei officially espouses reunification but does not accept terms offered by Beijing, insisting that China first adopt democratic reforms like those carried out in Taiwan.
A political impasse between Taiwan and China started in June 1995 after President Lee made a private visit to the United States, which Beijing saw as a move to promote independence.
After Lee's U.S. visit, Beijing suspended semi-official talks with Koo's foundation and launched the military exercises which peaked ahead of Taiwan's March 23 presidential election this year.
Despite the chance for contact with Jiang and an easing of bilateral hostility in recent months, analysts said they did not expect major breakthroughs to emerge from the APEC summit.
"There should not be any surprising development in Taiwan-China relations at the APEC meeting," said Chiu Chao-ling, a reseracher at Taiwan's Academia Sinica.
"The two sides set very different conditions for resuming talks. They won't agree all of a sudden," Chiu said.
China demands that Taiwan drop its bid for a U.N. seat, which Taiwan refuses.

Because Taiwan insists that all communications be conducted through Koo's foundation and its semi-official mainland counterpart, the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait, analysts said private meetings between Koo and his Chinese counterpart were unlikely.

"It should not make too much difference to current Taiwan-China relations as Taiwan can't send very top-level persons to APEC and China has no excuse to complain," said Yang Ya-hui, head of the independent Chung Hua Institution for Economic Research.
"But at least relations won't turn worse," Yang said.
